questions.text: I rarely notice when someone is trying to impress a particular person in a group.
I readily step in to mediate disputes by imposing a resolution.
I reschedule plans without guilt when something more important or interesting comes up.
When I learn about suffering in a place I have never visited, the people affected matter to me.
I am attracted to opportunities where I can blend into a well-functioning team.
I feel energized when the group collectively turns a situation around.
I tend to feel settled even when circumstances around me are in flux.
I tackle administrative tasks on a regular schedule so they never pile up.
I notice that my emotional intensity ebbs and flows like weather systems rather than following a predictable pattern.
I feel that refining my personal aesthetic—in everything from clothing to home design—is a worthy pursuit.
The felt weight of another person's hardship stays with me long after the encounter.
When I feel betrayed, the shock and hurt land in my body like a physical blow.
I routinely choose the path of least resistance for myself, even if it requires more from others.
I feel confident making decisions on behalf of a group.
I value knowing exactly where I stand on a project at all times.
I notice when the pitch of a room changes because one dominant personality entered or left.
I experience emotional pain as a dull awareness that fades predictably over time.
Someone's continuing hardship rarely matters to me once the news is old.
I notice that I don't experience the emotional hangovers that others describe after intense days.
When someone shares good news, my own excitement can rival theirs in intensity.
I notice that people look to me to set the standard of effort in a group.
I sense when someone is listening with the intent to find a weakness in what is being said.
I rarely notice the social dynamics of who pays for what in a group.
I focus entirely on the task at hand and clean up everything at the end in one pass.
I thrive when I can respond to whatever the moment presents rather than sticking to a predetermined path.
I find deep satisfaction in making personal sacrifices for the benefit of my community.
The more I learn about what someone is going through, the stronger my wish to help them.
Others' hardships sometimes leave me without much wish to help.
Someone else's grief rarely makes me want to comfort them.
I tend to measure my worth by how much I've contributed to others, not by what I've accumulated.
I routinely offer to handle the least glamorous tasks in any group effort.
I tend to keep a running tally of my personal wins and review them when I need motivation.
I find it satisfying to bring order to something that was previously disorganized.
I often find that I help the group define what success looks like together.
I tend to be surprised when someone tells me about interpersonal tension I had not noticed.
I notice when someone carefully chooses words to avoid offending a specific person in the room.
